tldr: In humanoid whole-body motion tracking, decoupling explicit inverse-dynamics-based "motion tracking torques" from reinforcement-learning-based "balancing residual torques" achieves both accurate tracking of diverse motions and high robustness against external disturbances.
hero_caption: Comparison between conventional methods and the proposed DKWBC. Conventional methods (left) output target joint positions with a single policy to jointly solve tracking and balancing, which tends to shrink motions to prevent falling. In contrast, DKWBC (right) sums model-based tracking torques and learned balancing residual torques, faithfully reproducing reference motions without collapsing posture.
overview:
When making humanoid robots execute all kinds of human-like motions, the biggest hurdle is reconciling "motion tracking" with "maintaining balance without falling." Recent reinforcement learning approaches predominantly rely on end-to-end methods where a neural network outputs target joint positions for PD controllers to jointly handle tracking and balance. However, even for similar poses, required joint torques and dynamic demands differ drastically between mid-sprint and landing from a jump. Forcing a single policy to handle both complex dynamics and environmental adaptation makes learning difficult, often leading robots to prioritize stability and produce conservative, hesitant motions.

To address this, the authors focused on the equations of motion for floating-base systems (where the robot's base is not fixed to the ground). Joint torques can be cleanly decomposed into a "model-computable component that generates robot accelerations" and an "environmental wrench component that handles ground contact and external forces." Based on this principle, the proposed method "DKWBC" divides roles: a "motion tracking module" tracks reference motions via inverse dynamics feedforward and PD feedback, while a "residual policy" directly outputs additional torques via reinforcement learning to maintain balance.

Experiments evaluated data scaling on the large-scale BONES-SEED motion dataset, external force application to both hands, and load tests with backpacks and handheld weights. DKWBC significantly outperformed state-of-the-art whole-body tracking models like SONIC and FALCON in tracking accuracy and success rate. On a real Unitree G1 robot, it stably executed aggressive motions including deep squats, walking, and jumping strikes.
contributions: Proposed DKWBC, a whole-body control framework that explicitly decouples model-based motion tracking torques from reinforcement-learning-based balancing residual torques based on floating-base dynamics equations.

Designed the residual policy to take inverse dynamics components as observations and add torques directly at 50 Hz without passing through PD servos, allowing the policy to focus on learning intrinsic balancing skills rather than tracking corrections.

Demonstrated in simulation and on real hardware (Unitree G1) that a single learned balancing policy maintains high tracking accuracy and balancing performance across unseen motion datasets, added payloads, and hand disturbances.

sections.heading: Why Motion Tracking and Balancing Shouldn't Be Mixed
sections.summary: Points out the challenges of conventional whole-body control using a single policy to output target joint positions for tracking and balance simultaneously. Explains the core idea and contributions of DKWBC, which separates model-based tracking from learning-based balance corrections using the structure of the equations of motion.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to serve as physical platforms for general-purpose intelligence, controllers that can accurately and stably execute diverse whole-body motions are essential. Recent work has improved tracking performance using large-scale motion capture datasets and high-capacity models like Transformers and Mixture-of-Experts.

However, many existing methods (such as BeyondMimic and SONIC) rely on a setup where the policy network predicts PD target joint positions (e.g., at 50 Hz), which are then converted to motor torques (e.g., at 200 Hz). In this structure, a single policy undertakes both tracking and balance maintenance simultaneously. Here lies the pitfall. Even for similar poses, the required dynamic joint torques differ greatly depending on motion velocity and acceleration. Forcing a single policy to simultaneously learn these intense motion-dependent torques alongside balance adjustments for ground contacts and disturbances severely complicates the learning task. Consequently, the policy becomes risk-averse, producing conservative (shrunken) movements and sacrificing tracking accuracy to avoid falling.

This paper proposes "DKWBC." Examining floating-base dynamics equations reveals that joint torques decompose into two parts: a model-based component determined by state and acceleration, and an environmental wrench component arising from contacts and external forces. Following this physical intuition, DKWBC produces nominal tracking torques using explicit inverse dynamics plus PD feedback, leaving the reinforcement learning policy to learn only residual torques for balancing. By decoupling roles, the policy is freed from motion-specific torque computations and can focus on mastering general balancing skills shared across motions.

captions.F1: Comparison between conventional approaches (left) and DKWBC (right). In conventional approaches, the policy outputs target joint positions converted to torques via PD control, often sacrificing accuracy for stability. DKWBC adds balancing torques from a residual policy to tracking torques from inverse dynamics, balancing while preserving tracking accuracy.

sections.heading: Lineage of Humanoid Control and Where This Work Stands
sections.summary: Reviews four research contexts: whole-body motion tracking, hybrid model-based and learning control, residual tracking, and force-adaptive interaction. DKWBC distinguishes itself by distributing analytical runtime inverse dynamics and support residuals directly at the torque level.
sections.details:
Related work falls into four main streams:

- Whole-body motion tracking: Originating with DeepMimic, motion imitation learning has expanded to real-world deployments (BeyondMimic), large-scale data training (SONIC), and integrations with diffusion and world models. Rather than competing with these, DKWBC complements them by redefining the policy's physical output from position commands to support residual torques.
- Hybrid model-based and learning control: Traditional whole-body control (WBC) relies on dynamics to resolve contact constraints and center-of-mass (CoM) accelerations. While prior works have learned CoM acceleration corrections or used residuals for arm stabilization, DKWBC decomposes torques across all actuated joints. The learned residual compensates for contact forces and disturbances without requiring online contact-force optimization at runtime.
- Residual tracking and policy adaptation: Methods like HiLo and RobotDancing learn joint target offsets around reference motions, while others (like ASAP) use residual models to bridge sim-to-real gaps. DKWBC differs by running an analytical inverse-dynamics module concurrently at runtime, performing role separation directly at the torque level.
- Force adaptation and physical interaction: Approaches like FALCON and HAFO coordinate upper and lower body control, while SceneBot conditions on contact labels. DKWBC achieves whole-body tracking resilient to payloads and hand disturbances using only a single residual policy paired with inverse-dynamics feedforward, without requiring extra contact sensing or per-task tuning.

sections.heading: Designing Dynamics-Informed Decoupled Control
sections.summary: Explains the torque decomposition theory derived from floating-base equations of motion, followed by the structure of the tracking module (inverse dynamics + PD feedback) and the reinforcement learning policy that outputs residual torques directly.
sections.details:
### III-A Dynamics-Informed Control Decomposition
Consider a floating-base robot with $n$ actuated joints. Extracting the actuated rows from standard equations of motion, joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ can be written as:
$\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}} + \mathbf{h}) - \mathbf{S}\sum_{k}\mathbf{J}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{k}$
where $\mathbf{M}$ is the inertia matrix, $\mathbf{h}$ comprises Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravitational terms, $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{k}$ are environmental external forces (such as ground reaction forces), and $\mathbf{J}_{k}$ are contact Jacobians. The first term represents nominal tracking torques computable from robot state and desired accelerations. The second term represents environmental wrench effects from contacts and external forces that are difficult to observe directly. DKWBC assigns the first term to an analytical model and the second term to a residual policy based on this physical structure.

### III-B Model-Based Motion Tracking Torques
The tracking module uses the recursive Newton-Euler algorithm (RNEA) to compute inverse dynamics feedforward torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{id}}$ from the current robot state $(\mathbf{q}, \boldsymbol{\nu})$ and reference accelerations $\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\mathrm{ref}}$. This decomposes into acceleration $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{acc}}$, Coriolis $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{cor}}$, and gravity $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{grav}}$ terms.
However, human-retargeted motions can be dynamically infeasible for the robot, causing drift with feedforward alone. Therefore, joint-space PD feedback torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{pd}}$ are incorporated. While PD torques account for less than 10% of total torques, they are vital for accurate tracking. Summing these yields tracking torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{trk}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{id}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{pd}}$.

### III-C Residual Learning for Balancing
The reinforcement learning policy learns additional balancing torques that tracking torques cannot provide. To prevent the policy from falling back on motion-specific tracking tweaks and instead acquire general balancing capabilities, key design choices are made in observations and actions:
- Observing tracking torques: The three inverse dynamics components ($\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{acc}}, \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{cor}}, \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{grav}}$) are included in the policy's observation. Showing the policy how much torque is already supplied by the tracking module helps it determine appropriate corrections.
- Direct torque output: Instead of predicting target joint positions at 50 Hz converted via high-frequency PD, the policy directly predicts residual torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{bal}}$ at 50 Hz with zero-order hold. Removing intermediate PD servos prevents the policy from exploiting high-frequency tracking error feedback to patch motion tracking, forcing it to focus purely on balancing torque corrections. Final joint commands are $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{trk}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{bal}}$.

captions.F2: Overall system architecture of DKWBC. The upper tracking module generates tracking torques from inverse dynamics (50 Hz) and position feedback (200 Hz). The lower residual policy takes inverse dynamics components as input and directly outputs balancing torques (50 Hz). Summing both torques drives the robot.

sections.heading: Superior Tracking Accuracy and Robustness to Unseen Motions and Forces
sections.summary: Demonstrates scaling performance on large-scale datasets, robustness against hand disturbances, ablation studies, and real-world results on a Unitree G1 robot. DKWBC outperforms existing baselines in tracking accuracy and versatility across all conditions.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 robot.

### IV-A Data Scaling Experiments
Subsets ranging from 2 to 128 hours were created from the BONES-SEED dataset and compared against state-of-the-art whole-body tracker SONIC. Evaluation metrics included success rate (fraction of time pelvis and end-effector height/pose errors remained below thresholds) and MPJPE (mean per-joint position error in millimeters).
As shown in Figure 3, DKWBC outperformed SONIC across all data scales. Even when trained on limited data (>= 4 hours), it surpassed the official SONIC checkpoint pretrained on over 600 hours in tracking accuracy. While success rates saturated near 100% as data increased, tracking error (MPJPE) continued to decline, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen motion categories.

### IV-B Tracking Under External Disturbances
Evaluating standing and walking motions under 3D time-varying forces applied to both hands, DKWBC was compared with FALCON and ResMimic. Scaling disturbance strength from 0x to 0.5x and 1.0x, DKWBC achieved the lowest upper-body joint position error (MPJPE), joint velocity error (MPJVE), and root velocity error across all levels, demonstrating superior disturbance rejection.

### IV-C Ablation Studies and Physical Interpretation of Residuals
- Value of decoupled control: Compared to BeyondMimic (coupled control), which achieved similar success rates, coupled control showed significantly worse tracking error due to overly conservative behavior. DKWBC maintained high tracking accuracy while preserving high success rates under payloads (5 kg backpack, 2 kg in each hand) and disturbances.
- Nature of residual torques: As shown in Figure 6, the learned residual torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{bal}}$ closely matches theoretical contact-compensation torques calculated from simulator contact wrenches, proving the policy genuinely learns contact compensation torques.
- Tracking module impact: Pure feedforward (FF only) resulted in a catastrophic MPJPE of 171.73 mm, but adding minimal PD feedback dramatically improved it to 4.45 mm, highlighting PD's necessity in absorbing retargeting dynamic infeasibilities.
- Real-world experiments: On a real Unitree G1, deep squats and walking with backpacks or dumbbells, as well as dynamic motions like dancing and jumping strikes, were executed stably using a single policy checkpoint trained entirely in simulation.

captions.F3: Training data scaling trends across two BONES-SEED test sets. Blue lines (DKWBC) achieve higher success rates and lower joint position errors (labeled values in mm) across all data scales compared to orange lines (SONIC).
captions.F5: Real-world motions on the Unitree G1 robot. Left: deep squats and walking under unloaded, backpack, and handheld weight conditions. Right: aggressive motions such as dancing and jumping strikes. All executed stably using the same policy checkpoint.
captions.F6: Comparison between learned residual torque (blue) and theoretical contact-compensation torque derived from environmental contacts (orange) during simulated running. Their amplitudes and temporal profiles align closely, showing that the residual policy successfully learns contact compensation.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: Summarizes the effectiveness of DKWBC in decoupling motion tracking from balance control. Explains how explicit inverse dynamics enables the policy to acquire general support capabilities, and outlines future extensions to richer physical contact tasks.
sections.details:
This paper proposed DKWBC, a humanoid whole-body control framework that decouples model-based motion tracking from reinforcement-learning-based support control.

By explicitly supplying tracking torques via floating-base inverse dynamics and joint PD feedback, the policy's learning task is reformulated into maintaining balance given reference tracking torques. This prevents the policy from being bogged down by complex motion-specific dynamics, allowing it to acquire core compensation skills to avoid falling. Simulation and real-world experiments confirmed significant gains in data efficiency, generalization to unseen motions, and robustness against disturbances and payloads.

As future work, the authors plan to extend this tracking-balancing decoupling approach to richer whole-body physical interactions and complex manipulation tasks.

takeaways: Instead of letting reinforcement learning handle everything, cleanly separating model-tractable tracking (inverse dynamics + PD) from contact-handling balancing at the torque level proves exceptionally effective.

Outputting balancing residuals directly as torques—rather than target joint positions through PD servos—prevents the policy from cheating via local tracking corrections, promoting motion-agnostic balance skills.
Explicitly feeding inverse dynamics components (acceleration, Coriolis, gravity) into policy observations substantially boosts zero-shot transfer and generalization to unseen motion datasets.
limitations: Does not fully resolve dynamic infeasibilities stemming from human-to-robot retargeting, retaining reliance on PD feedback gains within the tracking module.
While robust against disturbances and payloads, the study did not evaluate task success in explicit contact force control or manipulation, such as moving objects to target locations.
Because it relies on analytical inverse dynamics computations, robustness against significant model parameter mismatches (e.g., inaccurate link lengths or masses) requires separate validation.
